Biryar runs as two processes against one PostgreSQL: an API, which also
serves the interface, and a worker that does the fetching. The compose file
runs all three.

## What you need

**A computer that stays on.** Biryar runs on your own machine and can
only scan or reprice while it is awake. A laptop works for trying it; for
scheduled passes, a small always-on computer is better. These are all
fine:

| Machine | Notes |
|---|---|
| Windows 10 or 11 PC | 64-bit, with Docker Desktop |
| Mac | Intel or Apple chip, with Docker Desktop |
| Linux PC or home server | Docker Engine with the compose plugin |
| Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 | 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS, 4 GB model or more |
| A small rented server | Any Linux with Docker; nothing else runs on it |

**What it uses.** Nothing you would notice on a computer from the last
ten years: about 1 GB of disk for the program and its database, around 300
MB of memory while running, two processor cores. **No graphics card**, no
second machine, no account with us. An internet connection, because it
reads Amazon and your retailers.

**Docker.** The one thing to install first: [Docker
Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) on Windows and Mac, or
Docker Engine on Linux. On Linux, if `docker ps` answers "permission
denied", add yourself to the `docker` group and sign in again.

**An Amazon application**, if you want to connect a seller account:
[Getting your SP-API keys](/setup/sp-api/) walks through it. You can install
Biryar and look at a settlement file without one.

## Run it

Biryar is published as one container image, and one small file tells
Docker how to run it. Put it in a folder of its own and start it. The
lines differ only in spelling between systems.

**Linux and Mac**, in a terminal:

```bash
mkdir biryar && cd biryar
curl -fsSLO https://biryar.ciyalabs.com/get/docker-compose.yml
docker compose up -d
```

**Windows**, in PowerShell, with Docker Desktop running (`curl.exe`, not
`curl`: PowerShell's own `curl` is a different command):

```powershell
mkdir biryar; cd biryar
curl.exe -fsSLO https://biryar.ciyalabs.com/get/docker-compose.yml
docker compose up -d
```

That is all. Every time Biryar starts it gets itself ready: it creates or
updates the tables this version needs, and sets up `biryar_app`, the
restricted database account the program actually uses. That account
matters more than it looks: PostgreSQL lets its own owner account ignore
the rules that keep one business's data from another's, so Biryar never
runs as the owner. If the update ever fails, it changes nothing, and
`docker compose logs api` says why.

### After the machine restarts

You run those lines once. After a restart Biryar comes back by itself, at
the same address, as soon as Docker is running:

- **Linux**: Docker starts with the machine, and Biryar with it.
- **Windows and Mac**: Biryar starts when Docker Desktop does. To have that
  happen without opening it, switch on "Start Docker Desktop when you sign
  in" in Docker Desktop's settings, under General.

Give it a moment after switching on. Biryar waits for its database to
start before it answers, usually a few seconds. If the page still does not
open, `docker compose ps` in the `biryar` folder shows what is running, and
`docker compose up -d` there starts anything that is not.

## Your sealing key

On its first start Biryar makes the key that seals every Amazon credential
it stores, and keeps it on a Docker volume of its own (`biryar-keys`).
Nothing to generate, nothing to paste. **Keep a copy somewhere that is not
this machine:**

```bash
docker compose exec api cat /keys/sealing-key
```

Losing it means connecting Amazon again; anyone who has it can read what it
sealed. To move Biryar to another machine, or to bring a key of your own,
put it in a `.env` file beside the compose file as `BIRYAR_SECRET_KEY=`;
a key set there is used instead of the file.

## Settings you can change

None are needed. A `.env` file beside the compose file changes the port,
pins a version, or sets the database passwords; the example at
<https://biryar.ciyalabs.com/get/env.example> lists every line with what
it does.

## Your account

Open <http://localhost:8000> and choose **Sign up**. The first person to
sign up becomes the owner, and the page asks for this install's **setup
code**. The server prints it when it starts with nobody signed up:

```bash
docker compose logs api | grep -A 3 "setup code"
```

(Windows, PowerShell: `docker compose logs api | Select-String "setup code" -Context 0,3`.)
It also prints it on request:

```bash
docker compose run --rm api python -m biryar.init --setup-code
```

Then a username, your email and a password: twelve characters at least,
with one that is not a letter or digit, and a capital letter or a digit.

The next screen sets up **two-factor sign-in**. Scan the code with an
authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, Aegis,
1Password or Bitwarden all work) and type the six digits it shows. From
then on, signing in is your password and a code from the app. It is not
optional: Biryar holds the keys to your Amazon account, and Amazon asks
for multi-factor sign-in on any system that holds its data.

Anyone else in the business joins with an **invitation code** you make
under Settings, Team; the code already says whether they are an owner or
an assistant.

If you would rather make the owner from the shell, that still works:
`python -m biryar.init --email you@example.com` prints a generated
password, shown once.


The setup code is why the sign-up page is safe. A sign-up page on a
self-hosted install is a door onto the internet whose only job is to be
used once, and without a code whoever reached it first would become the
owner. With one, the person who becomes owner is a person who can already
read the server's log or run a command on it: the same authority as the
database itself.

## A forgotten password, or a lost phone

There is no reset email: a self-hosted install has no mail server, and
asking you to configure one for the day you forget a password is a worse
trade than a command. On the machine Biryar runs on:

```bash
docker compose exec api python -m biryar.passwd --login your-username
```

prints a new password, shown once (`--ask` prompts for one instead). For a
lost phone, add `--reset-two-factor`: it forgets the old authenticator,
signs that person out everywhere, and the next sign-in sets up a new one.

Passwords last a year; Biryar warns two weeks ahead and asks for a new one
when it runs out.

## Installing it as an app

Biryar is a web page, served by your own machine, and it can be installed
like an app: in Chrome or Edge, **Install Biryar** from the address bar or
the menu; in Safari on a Mac, **File → Add to Dock**. It then has its own
icon and opens in its own window. Nothing is downloaded or signed, and it
updates when the install does.

## Connecting Amazon

Everything is entered under **Settings, Connections**: the Client ID and
Client secret of your own private application, your merchant token, and
the refresh token the Solution Provider Portal gives you when you
authorise that application against your own account. Biryar seals all of
it on this machine and never shows it again.

The Client ID and secret are needed even though you paste a token: the
token is exchanged with Login with Amazon for a one-hour access token
before every read, and Amazon checks that exchange against the
application. Without them Amazon answers `invalid_client`, which looks
exactly like a revoked authorisation, so Biryar refuses to store a token
it could not exchange rather than letting you find out that way.

See [Getting your SP-API keys](/setup/sp-api/), which walks the private-
application path with screenshots.

## Seeing real figures before registering anything

You do not need an Amazon application to find out whether this is worth
your time. Sign in, and on the Portfolio page drop in a settlement report:
**Reports → Payments → All Statements** in Seller Central, downloaded as
**Flat File V2**.

Biryar reads it and shows you the period's revenue, what Amazon kept, and,
once you have loaded costs, what was actually left. **Nothing is stored.**
The file is read, the figures are shown, and none of it is kept, which also
means it cannot be double-counted against the feed later.

Two things it will tell you that are worth understanding:

- **Whether the file adds up.** The report states the payout Amazon made.
  Biryar adds up every amount in the file and compares. If they disagree it
  says so and tells you not to trust the figures, rather than showing a
  confident number read from a file it misunderstood.
- **Which fees it did not recognise.** Amazon publishes this report's
  column names but not the vocabulary of its fee descriptions, so a seller
  in an unfamiliar category will have some Biryar has never seen. They are
  listed, and they are still counted in the total, never silently dropped.

This is the fastest route to a real number, and it is the only one that
needs nothing from Amazon but a download.

## Getting to a profit figure

Connecting Amazon gets you **gross contribution**: revenue less what Amazon
and the carrier took. That needs nothing from you and appears as soon as the
first fetch finishes.

**Net profit needs one more thing from you: what the units cost.** Amazon
does not know, so Biryar will not guess. On the Portfolio page, upload a
supplier's invoice as a PDF (Biryar reads Müller, Saturn, MediaMarkt, NICI
and Qogita invoices, spreads the delivery over the units, adds the VAT you
cannot reclaim, and asks you which line is which product before saving
anything), or type a price under a product. For a whole cost book at once,
import a CSV, one row per invoice line:

```
vendor,doc_number,doc_date,name,qty,unit_price,sku,shipping,prices_include_vat,vat_rate
acme,INV-1001,2026-09-30,Widget Blue,5,8.40,MY-SKU-1,3.95,false,0.19
```

The `sku` column is your own Amazon SKU, and it is the one that matters:
Amazon's financial records name your SKU and nothing your supplier prints,
so a cost filed under an EAN is a correct number that no sale will find. The
import tells you about any row it could not read and any cost it could not
key to a SKU, rather than leaving you to wonder why a figure did not move.

Until every sold unit has a cost, net profit is left blank rather than
counting the unpriced ones as free, and the screen names the SKUs that are
missing one. See [How the fees are measured](/methodology/fees/) for why
that distinction is the whole point.

## Upgrading

```bash
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
```

The database is updated as Biryar starts. The API and the worker take
turns, so starting both together is fine, and an update that fails changes
nothing and stops with the reason in `docker compose logs api`.

`.env` says which version runs: `BIRYAR_VERSION=latest` follows releases,
and a number such as `BIRYAR_VERSION=0.1.0` stays on that release until you
change it. Every database update has a tested way back, should a release
need undoing:

```bash
docker compose run --rm api alembic downgrade -1
```

## Rotating the sealing key

Put the new key first and keep the old one, in `.env` (a key set there
replaces the one Biryar made):

```
BIRYAR_SECRET_KEY=v2:<new>,v1:<old>
```

Credentials move to the new key as each tenant is next used. Nothing has to
be re-encrypted in one go, and nothing stops working while it happens. Drop
the old key once every credential has moved.
